blocks.text: INNNEWS- If the first problem is the root of the learning foundation, then the second problem is due: that weak foundation now enters a productive age. At this point, education issues don't stop as school problems. It turns into economic, social structure, and nation endurance, which in turn could be a demographic bomb.

The demographic bonus has been treated like a spell for too long. It's as if when the number of working-age citizens is increasing, Indonesia will automatically jump into a developed country. But demographic bonuses aren't guarantees. It's just a window of opportunity.

A country can only turn demographic bonuses into dividents when the population of its age is healthy, educated, skilled, disciplined and relevant to economic needs. What's a age-work explosion if it's not a capacity, but a limitation?

That's where the second largest problem of Indonesia stands. We're entering a defining demographic phase with too many top 15-year-olds who are not quite ready to live and work in the modern economy. And the 21st century economy is no longer particularly focused on soil, raw materials, or just the number of people. It determines the quality of human capital.
Missing Potential 75 Percent

As discussed in the first part, Human Capital Index (HCI) Indonesia in 2020 is at 0.54. It means that the children born in Indonesia today are expected to reach about 54 percent of the productivity that should be achieved if they enjoy a full and healthy education.

It's been bad. But there's a deeper number: Utilization - Adjusted Human Capital Index (U-HCI) Indonesia is only 0.36. That is, after the quality of education and health are calculated, the potential goes down again when job market realities are included, because not all adults are completely absorbed and utilized efficiently.

Indeed, HCI and U-HCI are talking about children born today to project their productivity as they grow up. So 0.54 and 0.36 are not official numbers for the current Indonesian labor force, which was born about two decades ago. But that's exactly where the clue is. It makes sense that the Indonesian labor U-HCI is now lower than 0.36, maybe even below 0.30.

To be more concrete, let's use a simple illustration. Let's say about 50 percent of the population enjoys a relatively better education and health. In comparison, the proportion of labor educated SLTA or higher in 2025 according to the BPS is about 48 percent.
So let's say the first group average is only 30 percent of its productivity potential, and the second group is only 20 percent. The combined result is 0.25.

That is, the productivity that's actually achieved by average is only a quarter of the potential that it should have. The rest, 75 percent, lost on the road. Missing because of the quality of weak education, health isn't strong enough, and the job market hasn't been able to utilize humans efficiently.
And that, at a minimum estimate, is because the quality rate of education turns out to be worse than the duration of his education as the following deciphered.
Five Years Missing School

It seems to be brighter through Learning - Adjusted Years of Schooling, which is an old school that has been adjusted to the quality of learning. So what's measured is not just the duration of the school, but the learning capacity that's actually formed. This is where the quality of Indonesian labor portraits become more honest.

Nominal children who start school at the age of four can hope for 12.4 years of education. At first glance, it looked pretty good. Almost graduated from STTA. But once the quality of learning is calculated, the number is 7.8 years away, roughly the same grade 2 middle school.
So, almost five years of school at practice doesn't really produce the proper learning capacity. What a waste.

The findings are in line with OECD's survey of Jakarta adult literature. OECD shows that literacy skills and critical thinking graduates in Jakarta are no better than high school students in the developed world.
The same survey also found that nearly 70 percent of the adults in Jakarta are either at Level 1 or less in literation. It's not just a bad number. It's a sentence for low learning qualities.

At this rate, a person is generally able to read only short texts about familiar topics and find one very specific information. Structural arguments, nuances of meaning, and reasoning demands are not yet fully occupied.

That means, about 70 percent of the adults in Jakarta have not been able to understand the reading that demands reason. My estimate, for all of Indonesia, is that the number of people can reach 90 percent.

Let's use the SERS approach one more time. In 2025, about 90 percent of Indonesian labor forces were educated in the academy or less, or about 14 years of school. But if it's adjusted to the quality of education they receive, the average learning capacity is just the same as the third grade. At the same measure, Indonesian undergraduate graduates are roughly the equivalent of a sophomore high school student in terms of learning capacity.

This certainly isn't the size of all Indonesian individuals. It's a representational measure at a population level: the size of how formal education really changes, or fails to change, becomes ability.
Human Capital Transformation

That's where the issue is. Indonesia has schoololing, but it's not enough to produce learning. We've had a long study, but not enough to produce capacity. We have degrees, but we don't have common sense yet.

It's become far more problematic because the global economy is now reliant on the quality of human capital. Without adequate qualities, born not an explosion of productivity, but the swelling of informal work, the fragility of vulnerable work, the lower wages, and the growing social frustration. That's where the demographic bonuses turned into demographic bombs.
This is no longer just about basic literature. It's about competence, ability, productivity and innovation -- for fundamental, structural, chronic issues.

Therefore, the answer is not possible to be a projected project, a partial step, a slogan-laden policy, a trial program, momentary popularity, or a social aid quiz scheme that is busier to touch symptoms than roots, and more familiar with rente than results.

The solution is human capital transformation. And it has to be directed, precise, systematic and sustainable. As important as it is, that transformation must be designed by those who truly understand the problems and solutions above, not by those who smell the project faster than the problem.
